variants.name: Smart-reference proxy via std::shared_ptr / std::unique_ptr
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the smart-reference kind of the pattern: shared_ptr/unique_ptr/weak_ptr own the real subject and forward member access through operator->, adding sharing and lifetime policy on the way. Prefer this variant when the interposed concern is ownership and reference counting; choose the hand-written interface-forwarding class when the policy must run per call (authorization, lazy loading, caching) or when shared ownership is not the semantics you want.
pitfalls: shared_ptr cycles leak - a subject holding a shared_ptr back to the proxy needs weak_ptr; the control block is thread-safe but the subject is not.
operator-> must eventually yield a raw pointer and must not return a temporary: chained operator-> returns are re-applied until a real pointer appears.
Deref-style proxies expose the entire subject interface, including members you never intended to proxy.

variants.name: Classic interface-forwarding proxy class
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF structure written directly: the proxy implements the Subject interface, holds a reference or pointer to the real subject and forwards each operation explicitly, which is where virtual, protection and logging proxies put their policy. It compiles on any toolchain and keeps the proxied surface under explicit control, at the cost of mirroring the interface and updating the proxy whenever the subject changes. Choose it when the policy is per call, when the subject is not shared, or when C++11 smart pointers are unavailable.
pitfalls: Every subject method must be mirrored; a method added to the interface and not to the proxy either fails to compile (pure virtual) or silently bypasses the policy.
Holding Image& ties the proxy to the subject's lifetime - a proxy outliving its subject dangles; hold a smart pointer when the proxy owns it.
Copying the proxy copies the reference, not the policy state; decide explicitly whether proxies are copyable.
